messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marcus, a 35-year-old European American special education teacher, has been struggling with severe symptoms following a traumatic mugging that occurred six months ago. The incident left him feeling vulnerable and unsafe in his daily life. During the robbery, Marcus was confronted by an aggressive assailant who shouted threats and physically assaulted him, leaving him with neck pain that persists to this day. Since then, Marcus has been plagued by triggers such as shouting and the presence of authority figures like police officers, which send him into a state of intense distress. He experiences vivid flashbacks where he feels as if the traumatic event is happening all over again, and his neck pain becomes excruciatingly sharp during these episodes. These triggers not only bring back the memory of the mugging but also exacerbate his anxiety and hypervigilance. The photographic recall Marcus has of the event means that every detail is seared into his mind, making it nearly impossible to relax even in safe environments. He often scans for exits as soon as he enters any room or building, feeling the need to be constantly on guard. This constant state of vigilance feeds into his negative appraisals, reinforcing his belief that he is inadequate and should have been able to prevent the situation from escalating. When Marcus remembers the event, it evokes intense feelings of rage and guilt. The memory of being powerless and unable to protect himself intensifies his sense of inadequacy, leading him to believe that somebody else in his position would not have gotten into such a situation. These negative appraisals fuel his hypervigilance and make it nearly impossible for him to feel safe or relaxed. The cycle continues as Marcus’s threat perceptions are reinforced by his memories. He often finds himself scanning for exits during school meetings, where shouting can easily set off the traumatic memory of the mugging. His inability to relax in these environments has strained his relationships with colleagues and even impacted his teaching performance. For example, a recent incident at work where he overreacted to an administrator’s raised voice left him feeling humiliated and further convinced that he is inadequate. This, in turn, heightens his threat perceptions, making it harder for him to engage normally in professional settings. The more intense the memories become, the greater his sense of danger feels. What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a confrontation with his principal about his overreactions at work. He realized that his symptoms were affecting not just his personal life but also his career. Marcus is most afraid that he will continue to spiral into deeper isolation and be unable to manage his reactions in professional environments. At the same time, he hopes for strategies that can help him relax and feel safe again, restoring a sense of normalcy to his life. Through this journey, it has become clear that the trauma from the mugging is deeply ingrained in Marcus’s daily experiences, affecting how he interacts with others and perceives himself. His need to be constantly vigilant only reinforces his negative appraisals and triggers, creating a cycle of distress that leaves him feeling increasingly isolated and overwhelmed.
